newsitem.title: MEXICO: Controversial Mexican politician ensures succession.
newsitem.headline: Controversial Mexican politician ensures succession.

text.p: Mexico's ruling party may be heading for an election drubbing but strong economic growth, smart politics and opposition blunders seem to have assured it of victory in one key northern state.

In Sonora, a big, politically important state that borders Arizona, Gov. Manlio Fabio Beltrones enjoys approval ratings that turn others in Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) green with envy.

Polls now show PRI candidate Armando Lopez Nogales, a Beltrones protege, running more than 10 points ahead of his nearest rival, conservative businessman Enrique Salgado of the National Action Party (PAN).

"The people of Sonora know a good thing when they see it," said Beltrones in an interview with Reuters. He pointed to economic growth so strong it is attracting job-seekers from the rest of the country and a big public works programme.
Voters agree. Indemerc/Louis Harris, a polling firm, say Beltrones has a 68 percent approval rating. Some 60 percent of respondents want the next governor to continue his policies.

"They say he has done a good job with education, transport, water and health," said Vicente Licona, president of Indemerc. "They don't think he's done enough about drug trafficking or corruption ... but that's not a big concern."
Now, although the PRI nationally is likely to lose ground in congressional elections also to be held on July 6, the Sonora governorship looks safe.
As part of Mexico's industrialising northern border states, Sonora had seemed a perfect target for the PAN, which already governs neighbouring Chihuahua and Baja California.
With the opposition gaining still further in the wake of Mexico's 1994-5 economic crisis, many observers predicted a landslide PAN victory here.
Things looked better still for the PAN when a scandal hit Beltrones, leader of a younger generation of PRI hardliners known as "babysaurs" -- heirs to older party "dinosaurs."
The New York Times charged in February that Beltrones had allowed Mexican drug lords to set up a major trafficking operation in Sonora, which borders Arizona.

But Beltrones, who denied the allegations and sued the newspaper, emerged unscathed. His approval ratings even rose slightly after the affair because of Mexican resentment of interference in their affairs by the United States.
And the state's booming economy, which some allege is helped by laundering of illegal drug money, helped deflect criticism.

Meanwhile, the PAN was damaged by a scandal many believe was engineered by Beltrones himself. Dozens of top PAN members were found to have received favours from Beltrones' government, including copy machines and public vehicles.

Because of the scandal, the PAN scrapped its state convention, which was set to nominate for the race a popular former mayor of Sonora's second city of Obregon, Adalberto Rosas. Little-known Salgado was tapped instead by Mexico City higher-ups, angering many of the party's rank-and-file.

"Beltrones underhandedly put his people in the party to create a scandal ... it was necesary to clean house," Salgado, whose support has grown from the low teens to about 34 percent as his late-starting campaign got under way, told Reuters.
Asked about the allegations, Beltrones did not deny he had given favours to PAN officials and said the party's Mexico City leaders mistakenly blew the event out of proportion.
